stages.title: Five Things Before You Book
stages.description: The State Department's plan is a short list: learn the place, enroll, sort the documents, think about the activities, and buy insurance.
learningObjectives: Name the five planning steps
Add the advisory, local laws, and entry rules
State that the U.S. government does not pay your medical bills abroad

explainBack.question: A friend is about to buy flights and has only checked the weather. Using the State Department's international-travel planning page, list what they should open before they go, including the five checklist steps.
rubric: Before travel, use the checklist and review the Travel Advisory, local laws and customs, entry and exit requirements, visas, and embassy tips
The five checklist steps are learn the destination, enroll in STEP, sort documents, plan for personal needs and activity safety, and get travel insurance
The U.S. government does not pay medical bills or unexpected travel costs
Medicare and Medicaid usually do not cover care abroad
Buy travel medical insurance before the trip, including emergency care and medical evacuation

resources.title: International travel planning
resources.description: The official before-you-go list: the advisory, the documents, and insurance.
keyPoints: Before you travel, use the planning checklist and review the Travel Advisory, local laws and customs, entry and exit requirements, visa rules, and embassy tips
The checklist has five steps: learn about the destination, enroll in STEP, prepare your documents, plan for personal needs and the safety of your activities, and get travel insurance
The U.S. government does not pay your medical bills or unexpected travel costs abroad
Medicare and Medicaid usually do not cover care outside the United States
Buy travel medical insurance before the trip so emergency care and medical evacuation are covered

stages.title: Passport, Visa, and a Legal Medicine
stages.description: A passport can still have months left and be turned away. Some countries want six months of validity, and a U.S. prescription can be illegal abroad.
learningObjectives: Check passport length, including a child's five-year book
Find out whether the destination wants a visa
Treat a legal U.S. medicine as possibly illegal abroad

explainBack.question: An adult passport expires seven months after the trip, a child's passport is four years old, and a prescription pain medicine is packed in a pill case. Using the State Department checklist, say what to check before departure.
rubric: Check the passport expiration date early and apply early
A child's passport, for a child under 16, is valid for only five years
Some countries, especially in Europe, require at least six months of validity after your travel dates
Some countries require a visa or an electronic travel authorization; check the destination's embassy and the Travel Information entry and exit section
Some medicines that are legal in the United States, including prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, and narcotics, are illegal abroad
Check the health section, and bring copies of prescriptions and the original labeled bottles

resources.title: International travel checklist
resources.description: Passport validity, visas, and medicines that can be illegal at the destination.
keyPoints: Check your passport's expiration date early, and apply for a new one early
A passport for a child under 16 is valid for only five years
Some countries, especially in Europe, require the passport to be valid for at least six months after your travel dates
Some countries require a visa or an electronic travel authorization; check the destination embassy and the entry and exit section of the Travel Information page
Some medicines that are legal in the United States, including prescription and over-the-counter drugs and narcotics, are illegal abroad
Check the health section for the destination, and carry copies of prescriptions plus the original labeled bottles

stages.title: Tell the Embassy Where You Are
stages.description: STEP is free. It sends you security and disaster messages, and it gives the embassy a way to reach you.
learningObjectives: Say what STEP messages cover
Enroll with or without Login.gov
Name who the program is for

explainBack.question: A traveler thinks STEP is a paid service and that it is only for tourists. Using the State Department's STEP page, explain what it costs, what messages it sends, and who can enroll.
rubric: STEP is free
You can create an account or use a guest subscription without Login.gov
With Login.gov, you register the trip's location and dates and receive messages for that period
Messages cover security, demonstrations, health, weather and disasters, the Travel Advisory, and routine embassy services
Enrollment helps the embassy reach you or an emergency contact
The audiences named include tourists, business travelers, students, and long-term residents

resources.title: Smart Traveler Enrollment Program
resources.description: The free enrollment that lets an embassy reach you in an emergency.
keyPoints: The Smart Traveler Enrollment Program is free
You can create an account, or use a guest subscription without Login.gov
With Login.gov, you register where you will be and the dates, and you receive messages for that period
Messages include security alerts, demonstrations, health information, weather and natural disasters, Travel Advisories, and routine embassy-service notices
Enrollment helps the embassy reach you or an emergency contact
It is for tourists, business travelers, students, and long-term residents

stages.title: Insurance the Trip Actually Needs
stages.description: Medicare does not follow you abroad. Evacuation is a separate promise from a hospital bill, and you have to read what the policy leaves out.
learningObjectives: State what Medicare and Medicaid do not pay
Separate medical care from medical evacuation
Use the policy checklist before you buy

explainBack.question: A traveler has Medicare and a policy that pays hospital bills, and they are going somewhere with limited hospitals. Using the State Department's insurance guidance, explain the gap and what to check on a policy.
rubric: Buy travel health insurance; Medicare and Medicaid do not pay for care outside the United States
Ask your U.S. insurer what emergency and routine care it covers abroad
A short-term policy is an option, and some policies pay the hospital directly
Medical evacuation is strongly recommended, especially where care is limited, and it can be bought separately or as an add-on
Most policies cover care and transportation; read what a policy does not cover

Check the countries, the length of the trip, emergency care, transport back to the United States, travel and lodging expenses, emergency cash, current medical conditions, planned activities, and whether there is a 24-hour help line

resources.title: Insurance coverage overseas
resources.description: Why a U.S. health plan is not enough, and what an evacuation benefit is.
keyPoints: Buy travel health insurance before the trip; Medicare and Medicaid do not pay for care outside the United States
Ask your U.S. insurer whether it covers emergency and routine care abroad
A short-term travel policy is one option, and some policies pay hospitals directly
Medical evacuation is strongly recommended where local care is limited, and it can be a separate policy or an add-on
Most policies cover medical care and transportation; read both what is covered and what is excluded

Before you buy, check the countries on the itinerary, the length of the trip, emergency medical care, transport back to the United States, travel and lodging costs, emergency cash, existing medical conditions, planned activities, and a 24-hour help line

stages.title: Vaccines Weeks Before You Fly
stages.description: Routine vaccines first, then the destination list. Some vaccines need more than one dose, so the visit is four to six weeks out.
learningObjectives: Start with routine vaccines and the CDC destination page
Book the visit four to six weeks ahead
Get yellow fever vaccine only from an authorized center

explainBack.question: Someone leaves in ten days and has never looked up the destination. Using CDC's travel-vaccine page, say what to be current on, when to see a clinician, and where a yellow fever vaccine has to come from.
rubric: International travel raises the chance of diseases that are rare or absent in the United States
Be up to date on routine vaccines, and check the CDC page for the destination
See a clinician or travel-health specialist at least four to six weeks before departure, because some vaccines need more than one dose
Bring official immunization records
Malaria prevention pills, if prescribed, are taken before, during, and after travel
If yellow fever vaccine is recommended or required, it must come from an authorized U.S. yellow fever vaccine center

resources.title: Need travel vaccines? Plan ahead.
resources.provider: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.description: Why the vaccine visit happens weeks before departure, and who can give yellow fever vaccine.
keyPoints: International travel increases the chance of getting diseases that are rare or not found in the United States
Be up to date on routine vaccines, and check the CDC destination page for vaccines, medicines, and health risks
See a healthcare provider or travel-health specialist at least four to six weeks before you leave; some vaccines need more than one dose, so go as soon as you can
Bring a copy of your official immunization records
Malaria prevention medicine, if prescribed, is started before travel and taken as directed before, during, and after the trip
Yellow fever vaccine, when recommended or required, must be given at an authorized U.S. yellow fever vaccine center

Possible vaccines on the page include COVID-19, chickenpox, chikungunya, cholera, flu, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, Japanese encephalitis, MMR, meningococcal, monkeypox, pneumococcal, polio, rabies, shingles, Tdap, tick-borne encephalitis, typhoid, and yellow fever

stages.title: Medicine in the Original Bottle
stages.description: The destination's law controls the medicine, not the U.S. prescription. Pack it in a carry-on, labeled, with extra for a delay.
learningObjectives: Check the destination and every layover
Pack original labeled containers in a carry-on
Dose by time since the last dose in a new time zone

explainBack.question: A traveler pours pills into an unmarked case, packs them in checked luggage, and plans to take the next dose at the usual local clock time. Using CDC's medicine page, explain what can go wrong and how to pack and dose instead.
rubric: The destination's law controls the medicine; a drug that is prescription or over-the-counter in the United States can be unlicensed or controlled abroad, and the consequences include confiscation and jail
Check the destination embassy and any layover countries; many countries allow about a 30-day supply of certain medicines but want a prescription or medical certificate
If a medicine is banned, ask the clinician for an alternative and a letter describing the condition and the plan
See a clinician four to six weeks ahead and bring immunization records; if the trip is longer than 30 days, insurance may pay only a 30-day supply at a time
In a new time zone, dose by the time since the last dose, not by the local clock
Extreme temperatures reduce effectiveness; pack enough plus extra for delays, in a carry-on, in the original labeled containers
Bring written prescriptions with generic names, leave a copy at home, and ask for a note for controlled substances or injectables such as insulin or epinephrine
Counterfeit drugs are common; use the medicine you brought, and buy abroad only in an emergency

resources.title: Traveling Abroad with Medicine
resources.provider: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.description: How to carry a legal U.S. medicine into a country that may not allow it.
keyPoints: The destination country's law controls medicines; a U.S. prescription or over-the-counter drug can be unlicensed or controlled abroad, and consequences include confiscation and jail
Check the destination embassy and any countries where you have a layover
Many countries allow a 30-day supply of certain medicines but require a prescription or a medical certificate
If a medicine is banned, ask the clinician for an alternative and a letter that describes the condition and the treatment plan
Make the appointment four to six weeks ahead and bring immunization records; on a trip longer than 30 days, insurance may pay for only a 30-day supply at a time
In a new time zone, take the next dose based on the time since the last dose, not on the local clock
Extreme heat or cold can reduce effectiveness; pack extra for delays, in a carry-on, in the original labeled containers
Bring written prescriptions that use generic names, leave a copy at home, and ask for a clinician's note for controlled substances or injectables
Counterfeit drugs are common; use medicine brought from home, and buy abroad only in an emergency

stages.title: Leave a Copy at Home
stages.description: The clinician needs the itinerary. Someone at home needs copies. The embassy has a phone number that works from overseas.
learningObjectives: Tell the clinician the trip, not only the diagnosis
Leave document copies with someone at home
Save the overseas embassy number

explainBack.question: A traveler has the vaccines and nothing else: no copies at home, no embassy number, and a flight longer than four hours. Using CDC's before-you-travel page, say what still has to happen.
rubric: Check the CDC destination page, stay current on routine vaccines, and see a clinician or travel-health specialist at least four to six weeks before departure
Tell that clinician about pregnancy, allergies, or chronic problems, the destinations, the lodging, the type of travel, the dates, and the planned activities
Take prescribed medicine as directed, bring only medicine from home plus extra for delays, and bring official immunization records
Airplane travel, especially flights longer than four hours, can raise the risk of blood clots, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Find out whether health insurance covers care abroad, and consider coverage for health care and emergency evacuation
Enroll in STEP, leave copies of the itinerary, contacts, passport, and other documents with someone at home, and carry emergency contacts
From overseas, the emergency number is 00 1 202-501-4444; from the United States or Canada it is 1-888-407-4747
A travel health kit can include prescriptions, a mask, insect repellent, sunscreen of SPF 15 or higher, and the insurance card

resources.title: Before You Travel
resources.provider: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.description: The appointment, the copies left at home, and the embassy phone numbers.
keyPoints: Check the CDC destination page, stay up to date on routine vaccines, and see a healthcare provider or travel-health specialist at least four to six weeks before you leave
Share special conditions, destinations, lodging, type of travel, timing, and planned activities so the advice can be specific
Take prescribed medicine as directed before, during, and after travel; bring only medicine from home, plus extra for delays, because counterfeit drugs are common in some countries
Flights longer than about four hours can increase the risk of blood clots, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Travelers usually pay hospital bills out of pocket; consider insurance that covers health care and emergency evacuation, especially for remote areas
Enroll in STEP, monitor travel advisories, and leave copies of the itinerary, contacts, credit cards, passport, and other documents with someone at home
U.S. embassies and consulates assist U.S. citizens 24 hours a day: 1-888-407-4747 from the United States or Canada, and 00 1 202-501-4444 from overseas
A travel health kit should cover the whole trip plus delays and, depending on the destination, a mask, insect repellent, sunscreen of SPF 15 or higher, and the health insurance card

stages.title: The Health Kit and the Copies
stages.description: Pack copies of the passport and the proof a border may ask for, plus a small kit: sanitizer, repellent, and sunscreen.
learningObjectives: List the documents to copy
Choose repellent and sunscreen from the page
Check what the destination allows you to bring

explainBack.question: The suitcase has clothes and a toothbrush. Using CDC's pack-smart page, name the documents to copy and three health-kit items the page specifies by ingredient or strength.
rubric: Build a travel health kit for items that may be hard to find, and check the CDC destination page for what that place requires
Check the U.S. embassy because some countries restrict which medications you can bring

Carry copies of the passport and travel documents, a U.S. emergency contact card, lodging, the home clinician, immunization records, yellow fever proof if required, prescription copies, health and travel insurance cards, a list of local hospitals, and the U.S. embassy or consulate
Keep a print copy and a digital copy of each document when you can
Hand sanitizer should contain at least 60 percent alcohol
Insect repellent should use an active ingredient such as DEET or picaridin
Sunscreen should protect against UVA and UVB and be SPF 15 or higher
Check TSA for medicines and devices allowed in the cabin, check State Department customs and import restrictions, and enroll in STEP

resources.title: Pack Smart
resources.provider: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
resources.description: Which papers to copy, and what belongs in a travel health kit.
keyPoints: Prepare a travel health kit for items that may be hard to find, and check the CDC destination page for local health risks
Some countries restrict medications, so check with the U.S. embassy for that country

Carry copies of your passport and travel documents, a U.S. emergency contact, lodging details, your home clinician, immunization records, yellow fever proof if required, prescription copies, insurance cards, a list of local hospitals, and U.S. embassy or consulate information
Keep a print version and a digital version of each document when you can
Hand sanitizer in the kit should contain at least 60 percent alcohol
Insect repellent should use an active ingredient such as DEET or picaridin
Sunscreen should offer UVA and UVB protection at SPF 15 or higher
Check TSA rules for medicines and medical devices in the cabin, check State Department customs and import restrictions, and enroll in STEP

name: Travel Planning
description: Leave with the papers and the health plan already done: the State Department checklist, a passport that will be accepted, STEP, insurance that includes evacuation, and the vaccines and medicines the destination requires.
